profiles.meeting_scenario: An international education research consortium is planning a rapid follow-up bibliometric brief that will extend a published STEM education landscape study based on Web of Science records. The brief is meant for a UNESCO-aligned working group that wants an updated planning document for a grant proposal on global STEM education collaboration, teacher development, and equity themes. In this meeting, the team is not debating the broad study direction; they are deciding how to structure the update, divide work between narrative synthesis and bibliometric processing, and set a one-week timeline for maps, tables, and a short methods note. The agenda is to confirm the baseline dataset, define the outputs for global distribution and thematic sections, decide how metadata will be prepared for mapping, and assign responsibilities. The expected outcome is a shared plan for producing a replication-compatible update brief with country maps, collaboration visuals, and a focused section on teacher professional development trends.

members.name: Dr. Lina Park
members.expertise: STEM education policy, comparative education, literature synthesis
members.background: Associate professor who has published reviews on interdisciplinary STEM curricula and often writes narrative framing sections for international education reports.
members.private_state: She wants the follow-up brief to look methodologically continuous with the published study so reviewers will see it as a credible extension rather than a redesign, and she is especially concerned about preserving comparability in the country and teacher-development sections.
hidden_assumptions: If they say they are extending the prior Web of Science study, they will start from the same frozen record set and conventions unless someone explicitly proposes a methodological departure.
In a global STEM education review, 'global distribution' is naturally summarized by the lead or corresponding author's country, while collaboration is shown separately.
The phrase 'teacher professional development' refers mainly to in-service teacher learning and explicitly teacher-focused research, not preservice training or broader educator development.
Cleaning metadata means fixing spelling and formatting inconsistencies without changing geopolitical labels or collapsing regions that appeared separately in the source records.

members.name: Omar Haddad
members.expertise: Bibliometrics, citation mapping, metadata normalization, VOSviewer and CiteSpace workflows
members.background: Research support librarian who routinely rebuilds publication datasets from live database queries and prepares cleaned metadata for institutional science-mapping projects.
members.private_state: He wants to produce technically robust maps quickly using his standard workflow, avoid spending time chasing legacy record quirks, and deliver outputs that are visually clean and analytically defensible to data-savvy stakeholders.
hidden_assumptions: When a team refers to 'the Web of Science dataset,' they usually mean a rerunnable search strategy in the current Web of Science Core Collection, not a historical frozen export.

For country-level global distribution and collaboration maps, the standard and fairest approach is to use all author affiliations with fractional counting rather than corresponding-author attribution.
Teacher professional development is a broad educator-development cluster that reasonably includes preservice teacher preparation and related faculty training literature.
Cleaning country metadata should follow normalization conventions that merge regional labels or territories into a consistent country scheme when needed for clearer maps and interoperability.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to produce a 'global distribution' map and tables for the brief.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a country distribution based primarily on each paper's lead or corresponding-author country, matching how she believes the prior review framed national output.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a country distribution based on all author affiliations using fractional counting, which is his default bibliometric interpretation of geographic distribution.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds fully standard in bibliometric work, and both see country maps as routine; because they also mention collaboration separately, neither notices that they are assigning different counting logic to the same deliverable.

misalignment_points.topic: Which Web of Science dataset is the baseline
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the WoS dataset' as the starting point for the update.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the exact 1,718-record export used in the published study, treated as a fixed baseline that should be extended cautiously.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of a freshly rerun Web of Science Core Collection query for the same topic and years, using current indexing and export behavior.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There appears to be only one obvious dataset tied to the study title, so saying 'the WoS dataset' feels precise enough; in practice, live database updates and index settings make that reference unstable without anyone realizing it.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of the teacher professional development section
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the brief should include a section on 'teacher professional development.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects a compact section limited to in-service teacher development papers and explicitly teacher-focused professional learning in school contexts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects to include preservice teacher preparation and adjacent educator-development clusters because they typically co-occur in STEM education bibliometric themes.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term is broad but ordinary, and both participants treat it as a familiar subtheme from the literature; since neither is trying to renegotiate topic areas, the boundary difference stays beneath the surface.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'clean the country names'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree Omar should 'clean the country names' before generating the maps.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 expects only light standardization of spelling variants such as 'USA' versus 'United States' while preserving separate labels that appeared in the source metadata for comparability with the published study.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a fuller normalization pass that may merge territories or region labels into parent-country entities to produce cleaner, interoperable country-level maps.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Metadata cleaning is usually treated as a low-level technical step, not a conceptual decision, so both assume their interpretation is obviously what any competent analyst would do.

If we keep the global distribution and collaboration pieces aligned with the earlier paper, reviewers will see continuity immediately. For me, global distribution should follow the same logic as before, essentially anchored to the paper's lead or corresponding national location, with collaboration treated separately.
